title: The parish
hookLine: the local family of the Church

lines: THE BOXES ARE STILL TAPED SHUT.
cards: The boxes are still taped shut. Here's a small surprise for anyone who has moved: when a Catholic settles at a new address, Church law gives them a new parish along with it, before any registration form is filled in.
As a general rule, the law draws parishes by territory, so the street you sleep on decides which parish is yours.
The church down the road may have a bingo night, a youth group with a broken ping-pong table, and a priest who still hasn't learned your name. It's yours anyway.

teach.b: Back on day ninety-seven, you walked through a parish door. Today, what a parish is. The word often means the building, the brick church with the parking lot.

The Code of Canon Law describes something else: a community of the Christian faithful, set up for good, within a particular church, whose pastoral care is entrusted to a pastor under the bishop's authority.
A community first; the building is where it gathers. How do you belong? As a general rule, the Code says, a parish is territorial: it takes in all the faithful who live within its borders.
There are also personal parishes, formed around a rite, a language or a nationality, so a Spanish-speaking or Vietnamese-speaking community may have a parish that crosses the map.
But the default is simple: you belong where you live. What happens there?

The Book of Acts describes the first believers in Jerusalem, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Teaching, the breaking of bread, prayer. A parish is where those happen within reach of your front door: baptisms and funerals, confessions on Saturday, the Sunday Mass, a food pantry in the basement.
And why it matters on a Tuesday: a parish isn't chosen for its music or its preacher, though some people do shop around.
That means sharing a pew with people you didn't pick, and that is part of what makes it a family.

how: Catholics normally belong to the parish where they live, and register there for the sacraments and parish life. Personal parishes also serve people of a particular rite, language or nationality.

games.q: you've just moved across town. you liked your old parish. which parish are you in now, by the general rule?
o: your old one, until you write a letter.
the one whose territory you now live in.
games.why: the Code says parishes are, as a general rule, territorial. people can and do worship elsewhere, but the default parish is the one where you live.

practice: Bring to mind the parish nearest where you live, whether you go there or not: its doors, its steps, the people who come and go. If you pray, pray for the people inside it this week, by name if you know any.
If you don't, hold them in mind with a little goodwill.

wordCard.voice: Parish. The local family of the Church: a community of the faithful, usually drawn by where they live, cared for by a pastor under the bishop. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: home base. The street you sleep on already gave you one. See you tomorrow.
